Get started with powerape in Stata

Source: vignettes/articles/stata.Rmd
stata.Rmd

In a probit or logit model the coefficient is not the quantity anyone interprets. Conclusions are stated in probability points: the treatment raises take-up by ten percentage points. That quantity is the average partial effect (APE), and it depends on all coefficients and on the covariate distribution, so power tools that work in coefficient units cannot say how many observations are needed to detect it. powerape states the effect in APE units and simulates the whole study: it draws covariates and outcomes, fits the model, computes the APE with a delta-method confidence interval, and checks a claim on that interval (Riesthuis, 2024):

  • minimum: the lower bound of the interval exceeds the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), so the effect is meaningfully large. This is the default claim.
  • detect: the interval excludes zero.
  • equivalence: the interval lies inside (−SESOI, +SESOI), so the effect is too small to matter.

The Stata command powerape is a port of the R package of the same name and is documented side by side with it on this site. This page takes the six steps of the R article Powering the minimum-effect claim through Stata, in the same world, and then shows what is specific to Stata: who fits the simulated studies, and how to start from pilot data.

Installation 

net install powerape, from("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jespernwulff/powerape-stata/main/")
mata: mata mlib index
powerape version

net install copies the command, its help file and its Mata library; mata: mata mlib index makes the new library known to the running Stata session (needed once, right after installing); powerape version checks that the command and the library belong together. To update, add replace to net install. net get powerape, from(...) with the same address copies two files into the current folder: showcase.do, a guided tour of every subcommand, and build.do, which recompiles the Mata library.

Stata 16 or later is required. The control-function route for endogenous treatments uses cfprobit (Stata 18 or later), and computing interaction effects with ginteff itself, an option, needs that command from the Stata Journal (net install st0711, from(http://www.stata-journal.com/software/sj23-2)). The command has been tested on StataNow 19.5. After installation, help powerape opens the help file, which is also on this site.

Step 1: describe the world

One command describes the data-generating process (DGP) the study will sample from and stores it under a name, the way estimates store stores results. Here: a probit model, a binary treatment given to half the sample, two covariates, an outcome rate of 0.30 without treatment, and covariates that explain 15% of the latent variation.

powerape dgp d, focal(treat, binary p(0.5))                              ///
    covariates((age, normal mean(45) sd(12)) (female, binary p(0.55)))   ///
    correlation(0.2) baseline(0.30) signal(0.15)
powerape DGP -- probit
  focal: treat (binary, p = 0.50)
  covariates: age (normal, mean 45.00, sd 12.00), female (binary, p = 0.55)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.150
  target effect not set yet - run powerape setape or powerape setaie.

Each variable is written as (name, type options): binary p() or normal mean() sd(). The nuisance side is set on two friendly scales, the baseline outcome rate (baseline()) and the covariates’ latent pseudo-R² (signal()), and powerape solves for the coefficients that produce them. correlation() sets the latent correlation among the focal variable and the covariates. A pilot data set or a fitted pilot model can take the place of these guesses; see Pilot data below.

Step 2: pin the true APE

Suppose prior evidence suggests a true effect of ten percentage points, and effects below five points would not justify the program: the planning value is 0.10 and the SESOI is 0.05.

powerape setape d, target(0.10)
powerape DGP -- probit
  focal: treat (binary, p = 0.50)
  covariates: age (normal, mean 45.00, sd 12.00), female (binary, p = 0.55)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.150
  true APE pinned at + 0.1000 (beta_focal =    0.2943, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.400)

powerape setape solves for the coefficient of the treatment that makes the true APE exactly 0.10, given everything else, and refuses with an explanation when the target cannot exist (an APE of +0.40 at a baseline rate of 0.85, say). For interaction designs powerape setaie pins the average interaction effect instead; see Interaction effects.

Step 3: power for the claim 

powerape power d, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(1)
powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 500
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)
  power = 0.652 (MCSE 0.021)
  outcomes: minimum 0.652 | detect-only 0.338 | inconclusive 0.010 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

In each of the 500 replications powerape drew a sample of 1,500 observations, fitted it, and asked whether the 90 percent confidence interval of the APE lies above the SESOI (a one-sided test at the 5 percent level). It did in 65.2 percent of them. The line beginning fit: says who fitted the simulated studies: Stata’s own probit, with the APE and its standard error computed from e(b) and e(V) exactly as margins computes them.

Read the outcome distribution, not only the power. About a third of the studies would show an effect different from zero but could not claim that it clears the SESOI (“detect-only”): exactly the inconclusive result that a power analysis for detection alone hides. The R article finds the same split in the same world, up to simulation error.

Every subcommand stores its results in r().

return list

          r(is_margin) =  0
                r(mde) =  .
       r(nsim_confirm) =  .
          r(confirmed) =  0
               r(goal) =  .
           r(n_failed) =  0
           r(min_cell) =  206.746
          r(separated) =  0
             r(target) =  .1
              r(sesoi) =  .05
               r(conf) =  .9
              r(alpha) =  .05
               r(nsim) =  500
                  r(n) =  1500
               r(mcse) =  .0213023942316351
              r(power) =  .652

macros:
                r(fit) : "probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)"
            r(effects) : "closed"
             r(engine) : "stata"
                r(dgp) : "d"
         r(separation) : "fail"
                 r(se) : "model"
              r(model) : "probit"
           r(estimand) : "ape"
              r(claim) : "minimum"
               r(kind) : "power"
               r(name) : "_last"

matrices:
           r(outcomes) :  1 x 5

Results also stay available by name: powerape list shows the stored DGPs and results, and the option name() keeps a result under a name of your choice (see Justified alpha for a use).

Step 4: required sample size and the power curve

powerape n searches for the sample size that reaches the target power, then confirms it with a high-precision run and moves it upward, never down, if the confirmation falls short.

powerape n d, power(0.80) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(2) engine(mata)
powerape required sample size -- minimum claim
  n = 2103 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.808, MCSE 0.009)
  assumed true APE + 0.1000, sesoi 0.050,     90% CI (alpha =    .05), probit
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 2000.

A search runs thousands of simulated studies (here the confirmation stage alone ran 2,000), so this call uses the Mata engine, engine(mata), a self-contained port of the R package’s fitting routine that is many times faster than calling probit. Engines below explains the choice. The search took 13 seconds.

A power curve evaluates a list of sample sizes on the same footing.

powerape curve d, n(500(500)3000) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05)             ///
    nsim(300) seed(3) engine(mata)
powerape power curve -- minimum claim, probit (APE), nsim = 300 per point
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)

         n     alpha    power     mcse   failed  separated
       500    0.0500   0.3267   0.0271   0.0000     0.0000
      1000    0.0500   0.5267   0.0288   0.0000     0.0000
      1500    0.0500   0.6667   0.0272   0.0000     0.0000
      2000    0.0500   0.7567   0.0248   0.0000     0.0000
      2500    0.0500   0.8700   0.0194   0.0000     0.0000
      3000    0.0500   0.8800   0.0188   0.0000     0.0000

r(results) holds the curve as a matrix, ready to plot:

matrix C = r(results)
svmat C, names(col)
twoway connected power n, yline(0.8, lpattern(dash))                      ///
    ytitle("Power") xtitle("Sample size") ylabel(0(0.2)1)

When n is fixed: the minimum detectable effect

Often the sample is given: the archive has the firms it has. powerape mde turns the question around and finds the smallest true APE that the claim reaches with 80 percent power, with the same confirmation stage as powerape n.

powerape mde d, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(6) engine(mata)
powerape minimum detectable APE -- minimum claim
  MDE =    0.1094 at n = 1500 for 80% target power (confirmed 0.797, MCSE 0.009)
  smallest effect demonstrably above sesoi 0.050
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 2000.

With 1,500 observations, the study can show an effect to be meaningfully above 0.05 if the true effect is about 0.109 or larger.

Step 5: how fragile is this to the contextual guesses?

The baseline rate and the covariate signal are guesses. powerape robust repeats the analysis over a grid of them and reports the worst case (Hancock & Feng, 2026). By default the APE is re-pinned in every scenario (pin(ape)), so only the precision of the estimate varies.

powerape robust d, n(2200) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05)                    ///
    vary(baseline(0.20 0.40)) gridpoints(3) nsim(300) seed(4) nonmax engine(mata)
powerape robustness sweep -- minimum claim, APE, pin = ape
  n = 2200, nsim = 300 per scenario, 3 scenario(s) over: baseline
  power range [0.793, 0.870]; worst scenario: row 3
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
 row     baseline    implied_eff    power     mcse separated
   1           .2         0.1000   0.8700   0.0194    0.0000
   2           .3         0.1000   0.8100   0.0226    0.0000
   3           .4         0.1000   0.7933   0.0234    0.0000

Dropping nonmax adds n_max, the largest required sample size across the scenarios, at 90 percent power by default (nmaxpower()): the sample size that insures the design against the guesses. mode(mde) reports the minimum detectable effect per scenario instead of power.

Step 6: the citable paragraph

powerape statement writes the last result as a methods paragraph for a grant application or a preregistration.

powerape power d, n(2200) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(5)
powerape statement
powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 2200, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 500
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)
  power = 0.816 (MCSE 0.017)
  outcomes: minimum 0.816 | detect-only 0.180 | inconclusive 0.004 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

We conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the average partial effect
(APE) of treat using the powerape package for Stata (version 0.1.2 (Stata port
of powerape 1.11.3)), following the confidence-interval approach of Riesthuis
(2024). The assumed data-generating process was a probit model with focal
variable treat (binary, prevalence 0.50); parametric covariates age
(continuous, mean 45, SD 12), female (binary, prevalence 0.55), with an
exchangeable latent (Gaussian-copula) correlation of 0.20 among the focal
variable and the covariates; baseline outcome rate 0.300 with the focal at
reference; nuisance covariates contribute a latent pseudo-R-squared of 0.15.
The assumed true APE was 0.100 (10.0 percentage points). At a sample size of n
= 2200, simulated power for the minimum-effect claim (the 90% confidence
interval's lower bound exceeding the smallest effect size of interest, 0.050;
a one-sided test at alpha = 5%) was 0.816 (Monte Carlo SE 0.017; 500
replications). Across replications, the probability of concluding a meaningful
effect was 0.816, of detection without meaningfulness 0.180, of an
inconclusive result 0.004, and of equivalence 0.000. Estimation used maximum
likelihood with delta-method Wald confidence intervals; replications without a
maximum-likelihood estimate, from a failed fit or from separation (a focal
cell with no events or no non-events), counted against the claim (0.0% of
replications).

Engines: who fits the simulated studies

The simulation draws the data in Mata. Fitting each simulated study can be left to Stata or done in Mata:

  • engine(stata), the default, writes every simulated study to a temporary frame and fits it with Stata’s own probit or logit, with vce(cluster) for panels and cfprobit for endogenous treatments. The effects are computed from e(b) and e(V) by the closed-form delta method that margins uses.
  • engine(mata) fits each study with a Mata port of the R package’s routine (Fisher scoring, expected information).

On the same seed both engines draw the same studies, so they can be compared directly:

powerape power d, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(1) engine(mata)
powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 500
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  power = 0.652 (MCSE 0.021)
  outcomes: minimum 0.652 | detect-only 0.340 | inconclusive 0.008 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

The power is the same, 0.652. The outcome split differs by one study of 500, because probit computes standard errors from the observed information and the Mata engine from the expected information, which moves an interval that sits right at a boundary. The Mata engine took 1.5 seconds, probit 20.8. Use the Mata engine for searches, curves and sweeps, and confirm the final design with Stata’s estimator.

effects(margins) goes one step further and computes every APE with margins itself (or with ginteff for interaction effects). On the same seed it reproduces the closed-form results exactly:

powerape power d, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(100) seed(7)

powerape power d, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(100) seed(7)   ///
    effects(margins)
powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 100
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)
  power = 0.720 (MCSE 0.045)
  outcomes: minimum 0.720 | detect-only 0.260 | inconclusive 0.020 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 100
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(margins)
  power = 0.720 (MCSE 0.045)
  outcomes: minimum 0.720 | detect-only 0.260 | inconclusive 0.020 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

It is also slower (8.9 against 3.0 seconds for these 100 replications), so its use is as a check. engine() and effects() given on one command apply to that command only; powerape engine shows and sets the defaults for the session:

powerape engine
powerape engine, engine(mata)
powerape engine, engine(stata) effects(closed)
engine(stata) effects(closed)

engine(mata) effects(closed) set as the session default

engine(stata) effects(closed) set as the session default

Pilot data

When pilot data are available, the covariates can come from them instead of from parametric guesses. Here is a small simulated pilot:

set seed 20261016
set obs 500
generate treat  = runiform() < .5
generate age    = rnormal(45, 12)
generate female = runiform() < .55
generate y      = runiform() < normal(-0.9 + 0.3*treat + 0.01*age + 0.2*female)

empirical resamples whole rows of the pilot data in memory and calibrates the outcome model to the stated baseline rate and signal. A listed focal variable is resampled jointly with the covariates; one specified as (name, binary p()) is drawn independently of them instead.

powerape dgp pilot_rows, empirical focal(treat) covariates(age female)    ///
    baseline(0.30) signal(0.15)
powerape setape pilot_rows, target(0.10)
powerape power pilot_rows, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(11)
powerape DGP -- probit (empirical covariates)
  focal: treat (binary, p = 0.49) [resampled jointly with covariates]
  covariates: age, female
  pilot rows: 500 (resampled with replacement)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.150
  target effect not set yet - run powerape setape or powerape setaie.

powerape DGP -- probit (empirical covariates)
  focal: treat (binary, p = 0.49) [resampled jointly with covariates]
  covariates: age, female
  pilot rows: 500 (resampled with replacement)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.150
  true APE pinned at + 0.1000 (beta_focal =    0.2940, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.400)

powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 500
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)
  power = 0.656 (MCSE 0.021)
  outcomes: minimum 0.656 | detect-only 0.330 | inconclusive 0.014 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000

fromfit takes the world from a fitted probit or logit model: the nuisance coefficients and the pilot rows come from the fit, and setape re-solves the focal coefficient for the planning value. baseline() can override the pilot’s outcome rate.

probit y treat age female, nolog
powerape dgp pilot_fit, fromfit focal(treat)
powerape setape pilot_fit, target(0.10)
powerape power pilot_fit, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(500) seed(12)

  focal: treat (binary, p = 0.49) [resampled jointly with covariates]
  covariates: age, female
  pilot rows: 500 (resampled with replacement)
  pilot model: probit y treat age female (nuisance coefficients lifted; focal coefficient re-solved)
  baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.358, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.024
  target effect not set yet - run powerape setape or powerape setaie.

  focal: treat (binary, p = 0.49) [resampled jointly with covariates]
  covariates: age, female
  pilot rows: 500 (resampled with replacement)
  pilot model: probit y treat age female (nuisance coefficients lifted; focal coefficient re-solved)

  true APE pinned at + 0.1000 (beta_focal =    0.2614, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.458)

  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 500
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)

The R functions for the two routes are ape_dgp_empirical() and ape_dgp_from_fit(). Panel data and endogenous treatments have their own routes, panel and iv; see Panel designs and IV designs.
